summary: A 50-foot stone daymark of 1827 on uninhabited Little Mark Island in Casco Bay, Maine, with a shipwreck refuge room; a beacon was added in 1927 and the light was deactivated in 2019.

structures.note: Pyramidal daymark, 50 ft (15 m) tall, 18 ft square at the base; rock rubble in lime mortar (NRHP). Rowlett's directory says dressed granite blocks. Interior room about 12 ft a side, open to the top; concrete cap and beacon added 1927.

staffing.note: No keeper ever lived here (Rowlett; the 1932 list says unattended). Beacon powered by batteries recharged by a solar array.

access.note: Uninhabited island, federal (Coast Guard) property, reached only by boat; the sources describe no public landing. Transfer offered in 2023; no decision reported as of August 2025.

facts.agency: United States Coast Guard (Aids to Navigation Team, Station South Portland); federal transfer offered 2023 through the National Park Service (Harpswell Anchor, 2025)

events.note: Maine (26 February 1825) and Massachusetts (11 June 1825) legislatures passed resolves supporting a transfer of the island; the reason is unclear.
Authorized 2 March 1827 with a $1,200 appropriation; completed late 1827 at a final cost of $1,065.54.
Deed dated 9 May 1827 transferred the island to the United States for twenty dollars.
Maine legislature ceded jurisdiction over the island (act approved 15 February 1828).
Fiscal year ended 30 June 1900: Lighthouse Board report records the beacon as whitewashed.
Beacon light installed on top of the monument: a 200-millimetre optic burning compressed acetylene gas.
Rectangular concrete slab placed atop the tower and a steel guardrail installed.
Bureau of Lighthouses abolished; the Lighthouse Service assigned to the Coast Guard.
Acetylene lamp replaced by an electric lamp in the 1940s (year approximate; the nomination reads it from a cabinet in the tower).
Light described as 150 candlepower with eight miles of visibility, up from 90 candlepower in 1957.

National Register nomination certified for the Coast Guard in February 2016 (the form's signature date). The listing itself is not confirmed in the sources read (Wikidata gives 7 June 2016). The nomination says the light was still functioning.
Rowlett's Lighthouse Directory: the light was deactivated in 2019 and the monument is again a daybeacon.
Federal government declared the island and monument excess and offered them at no cost to an eligible municipality or nonprofit; not transferred.
August 2025: Harpswell and The Presumpscot Foundation still pursuing the offer; federal cutbacks had slowed the process.

notes_for_editor: 1. Status conflict: the 2016 nomination says the light still functions (p. 9); Rowlett's directory says it was deactivated in 2019 (p. 6 source); the Harpswell Anchor (Sept 2023) says 'no longer in operation'. No Coast Guard light list after 2015 was read. Check the current Coast Guard Light List before publishing 'deactivated 2019' as settled. 2. Tower height: the 1936 Lighthouse Service Bulletin says 'about 60 feet'; the nomination and the 2023 newspaper say 50 feet; the story uses 50 and states the Bulletin figure. 3. Stone: the nomination says rock rubble, probably local; Rowlett says dressed granite. Both are stated; not resolved. 4. Position: the 2015 light list quoted in the nomination gives 43-42-32.1 N, 070-01-51.9 W, about 25-30 m from the record's point (43.709167, -70.031389). Not changed; within normal error. 5. The nomination gives 'southwest' of Bailey Island in its cover and Section 7 and 'southeast' in another passage; the story uses 'northern Casco Bay' and does not give a bearing. 6. The 2016 listing date (7 June 2016, from Wikidata and the record) is not printed on the nomination pages read; the form bears April 2016 receipt stamps. 7. Keepers: the USLHS place record lists no roster; the monument was unattended, so the keepers chapter is omitted. 8. Storms and wrecks: no dated wreck or rescue at this monument appears in the sources read; the corpus greps (lhb, lss, bulletin) found only the 1900 whitewash and the 1936 Bulletin description. The shipwreck refuge is a design purpose, not a recorded event. 9. Blunt's American Coast Pilot (1847) is read only as quoted in the nomination; the original was not read. 10. Rowlett's directory credits a 'Mariner's Refuge' name to Edward Rowe Snow; not used. 11. No newspaper search was run for this station (budget). A search for the 1927 beacon or the 2019 deactivation in Maine newspapers could settle the status and the 1927 date. 12. Owner: the nomination says Coast Guard; the 2025 Anchor says the offer runs through the National Park Service. Status as of October 2026 not found in search results.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1936 Lighthouse Service Bulletin says about 60 feet; the nomination and the 2023 Harpswell Anchor say 50 feet, and Rowlett says about 50 feet. The story uses 50 feet and reports the Bulletin's figure in the text.
